model.title: At rest a pupil breathes 15 times per minute with a tidal volume of 500 cm³. After exercise: 28 breaths per minute, 1100 cm³. How many times greater is the ventilation rate after exercise?

questions.q: Describe what happens when you breathe in. [4 marks]
questions.a: External intercostals contract, ribs up and out (1); diaphragm contracts and flattens (1); thorax volume increases (1); pressure decreases below atmospheric so air flows in (1).
questions.model: Muscles: intercostals and diaphragm contract. Movement: ribs up and out, diaphragm flattens. Volume: increases. Pressure: falls. Air: flows in from higher pressure.

questions.a: Large surface area; walls one cell thick; rich capillary network (also moist).

questions.q: Why does ventilation keep the gradient steep?
questions.a: Fresh air brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Core: Label the thorax diagram (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, ribs, intercostals, diaphragm, pleural membranes).
questions.a: Correct labels on the portal diagram.
questions.model: Teacher labels the trachea first: windpipe held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage.

questions.q: Extend (home practical, 4SD0 2.50): Count breaths per minute at rest and after 1 minute of gentle stepping. Explain the change. [3 marks]
questions.a: Rate rises (1); muscles respire faster, needing more oxygen (1) and producing more carbon dioxide to remove (1).

questions.q: Stretch: Ventilation rate = breaths per minute × tidal volume. 15 breaths, 0.5 dm³: calculate.
Big question: how do your lungs keep your blood topped up with oxygen?
questions.a: Ventilation brings fresh air to the alveoli, which are adapted for fast diffusion into the blood.
